**RESEARCH ARTICLE - ­METHODOLOGY**
# **PredictPP: A Rank- ­Based Weighted Ensemble Model for ** **Prediction of Software Project Productivity**

**1   |   Introduction**

In modern times, software has become an integral component
of virtually every occupation inside the workplace. Software
is ubiquitous in various industries, from healthcare and food
to defense, suggesting that the growing population relies
on high- ­quality software that generates accurate outcomes.
Nevertheless, creating a prosperous software project poses a significant challenge within a software organization. According to
the Standish Group report issued in 2020, the success rate of software projects was 31%, although 50% of projects were classified
as challenging, and the remaining 19% were deemed failures [1].

© 2025 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.


Insufficient knowledge of requirements and inaccurate size calculation are primary factors contributing to software failure [2].
These factors prompted academics to investigate the estimate of
software for accurate assessment of size and effort.

Software effort estimation (SEE) is a crucial requirement
during the preliminary phase of a project to allocate appropriate resources [3]. Given the limited availability of information at this stage, the managers prioritize estimating the size.
The size measures can be helpful to provide valuable insights
into estimating the potential effort required. Various methodologies have been devised in previous years leading up to the


*Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025; 37:e70059 1 of 16
[https://doi.org/10.1002/smr.70059](https://doi.org/10.1002/smr.70059)

establishment of the function point (FP) [4] and the constructive cost estimation (COCOMO) [5] techniques to estimate
size. Nevertheless, the utility of FP and COCOMO approaches
is diminished when considering vulnerabilities associated
with parameters such as FPs and line of code (LOC) in the
respective cases. Moreover, it should be noted that these methodologies are mostly applicable to software systems produced
using procedural programming paradigms rather than the
more contemporary object- ­oriented software development
approaches.

The object- ­oriented (OO) development paradigm has garnered
significant attention because of the inherent dynamism and
reusability offered by programs written in OO programming
languages, a feature absent in procedurally generated software. Use case diagrams have been widely used in modeling
the functional requirements of OO systems, especially in contexts where structured analysis and early- ­stage planning are
essential. Their ongoing importance is apparent in scenarios
that require formal documentation, including academic projects, government systems, and enterprise- ­level software development. The use case point (UCP) methodology, based on use
case modeling, is an effective tool for early effort estimation
in these contexts. Although agile development approaches
typically prioritize user stories for their adaptability and ease,
our research is conducted in areas where structured estima
tion is essential, rendering the usage of use cases both suitable and advantageous for the aims of this study. Karner [6]
introduced the UCP strategy as a means of estimating the size
of OO software projects. This approach draws upon the fundamental principles of the FP technique. The UCP approach
considers UML use case diagrams as input for the UCP estimation. The use case diagram components, such as actors and
use cases, are converted into their related size measurements
to compute UCP value through a well- ­defined methodology.
The performance of the UCP approach relies upon the degree
to which the use case diagram is explained [7]. So, this technique is dangerous to use without sufficient data. Although
the UCP estimation technique requires less effort than the FP
technique, the UCP is not noteworthy as a proficient effort estimation inside organizations because there is no accord on
the best way to interpret the UCP size into a related measure
of effort.

As mentioned earlier, the UCP approach for SEE consists of two
steps: size estimation (in UCP) and effort estimation from the
calculated size. The software size can be easily calculated with
a well- ­defined procedure by Karner [6]. However, effort estimation from the UCP is a tedious task. Initially, Karner suggested
that the effort can be computed by multiplying UCP with the
predecided productivity value, as shown in Equation (1). This
methodology is somewhat transparent yet hazardous if the manager has less information about productivity. Productivity can
be computed by dividing effort by size [8]. This definition involves discussion because there is no standard on the best way
to refer to that relationship.

*Effort* = *Productivity* [∗] *Size* (1)

The productivity of a project is used as a cost driver for estimating effort using the classical UCP method. A few investigations


have been done in the past to compute software productivity before software effort; a restricted number of productivity values
are used in most of the studies [6, 9, 10]. These methodologies do
not provide any consideration for the project attributes. Karner

[6] recommends a single productivity value for all the projects,
20 person- ­h/UCP. In a few other studies, researchers predicted
the value of project productivity with the help of environmental
factors. Schneider and Winters [10] (S&W) have used three types
of productivity (very low = 36, low = 28, and fair = 20) values
based on eight environmental factors. Nassif et al. [9] have used
four types of productivity values based on eight environmental
factors and utilized an expert- ­based fuzzy model. Then, they
associate productivity with their nonlinear regression model
for computing effort. Similarly, Azzeh and Nassif [11] have developed a two- ­stage hybrid model for effort estimation utilizing productivity and show the utilization of classification and
clustering- ­based approaches for deriving different productivity
labels.

Based on the above discussion, we can observe the following findings concerning productivity. The assumption made
by Karner is not a practical methodology because it does not
consider the contrasts between software projects of their sorts,
surroundings, and multifaceted nature. The S&W model endeavors to group a project into 1 of 3 classes based on calculating environmental factors utilizing a particular counting
approach. The classification technique relies on counting the
factors, disregarding the impact of their values. Nassif et al.
calculated productivity values with the help of a prod_sum
variable, utilizing an expert- ­based fuzzy model. Maybe they
would have obtained better results if they had used some clustering approaches dependent on the gathered data. Similarly,
Azzeh et al. have used a hybrid model to classify productivity
labels, but the productivity values largely depend on the technique used to cluster and classify projects. This motivated us
to develop a naive method for project productivity prediction,
which can further estimate the effort required to create that
project.

Because a minimal amount of work has been done to consider

the advantage that can be acquired from predicting project
productivity, we have developed a rank- ­based weighted ensemble method, which we call PredictPP, for project productivity prediction based on environmental factors utilizing
various individual and ensemble learners. The individual

learners used for productivity prediction in the presented
work are simple linear regression (SLR), Least Absolute
Shrinkage and Selection Operator Regression (LR), ridge regression (RR), elastic net regression (ER), K- ­nearest neighbor
(KNN), decision tree (DT), support vector regression (SVR),
and multilayer perceptron (MLP). The hyperparameters of
these individual prediction models are tuned using the grid
search approach. These tuned individual prediction models
are compared to select the top five individual learning models
for project productivity prediction. The selected models will be
base learners to develop ten different homogeneous (bagging
and boosting) ensemble prediction models. The performance
of these ensemble prediction models will be compared to select the top three models, which will then be combined using
a ranking mechanism to obtain the proposed model. Then, we
compared the results of the proposed approach with those of


2 of 16 *Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025

the existing models used for productivity prediction. Based on
the above discussion, this research paper aims to answer the
following research questions (RQs):

  - RQ1: How does the proposed PredictPP model perform
compared to the base models to predict the value of project
productivity?

  - RQ2: Does the proposed PredictPP model generate better
predictions than other homogeneous ensemble learning
models?

  - RQ3: How does the proposed PredictPP model perform
compared to the existing models in the literature?

We have used the Western University dataset of 65 projects [9] to
address these inquiries and applied different models for productivity prediction and effort estimation. The significant contributions of this work are as follows:

 - Researchers have used project productivity as a cost driver
for estimating effort in existing works. They have selected
a project productivity value out of a set of predecided values. So, there may be a possibility that the productivity values of multiple projects will be the same even though their
nature is different. To handle this limitation, we propose
using learning models to predict project productivity based
on environmental factors. Hence, this paper aims to show
the usage of machine intelligence in project productivity
prediction, which can help estimate software efforts.

 - We have applied various individual and ensemble learning models for productivity prediction and evaluated these
models based on different performance measures. Further,
the performance of these models is compared against the
classical models such as Karner, S&W, and Nassif. The results show that the learning models perform relatively better than the classical models.

 - We proposed a rank- ­based weighted ensemble model for
project productivity prediction based on the above contributions. To our knowledge, no earlier work has been reported
using the ranking method for ensemble weight generation
to predict productivity.

 - We compared the performance of the proposed approach
with base learning models used in this study based on various evaluation measures. Also, we have validated the results by performing statistical analysis.

 - We have compared the performance of the proposed approach with the existing UCP prediction models available
in the literature.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses
the commonly used methods for UCP estimation and the existing work. Section 3 discusses the proposed approach utilized
for productivity prediction and effort estimation. Section 4
discusses the dataset, learning models, and performance measures used in this study. The results of the different models are
discussed in Section 4. The statistical analysis results and the
answers to the RQs are discussed in Section 5 and Section 6, respectively. Threats related to validity are discussed in Section 7.
Finally, Section 8 presents the conclusion.


**2   |   Background**

The background on classical methods for effort estimation using
UCP is provided in Section 2.1. Subsequently, Section 2.2 presents various existing works for UCP estimation.

**2.1   |   Commonly Used Classical Methods for UCP**
**Effort Estimation**

**2.1.1   |   Karner's Method**

In 1993, Karner introduced the UCP calculation approach to
estimate the size of object- ­oriented software projects [6]. This
approach utilizes use case diagrams for estimation. The computational efficiency of the UCP approach is contingent upon
the level of detail and clarity with which use case diagrams are
elucidated. Hence, adhering to the prescribed rules for creating
use case diagrams as outlined in references [12, 13]. The components of the use case diagram, including actors and use cases,
are transformed into their respective size measures to calculate
the UCP value using a clearly defined approach. Next, the calculated UCP value is modified by different technological and environmental complexity parameters.

The computation of the UCP can be facilitated by utilizing
four distinct elements. The initial component of UCP computation is determining the unadjusted actor weights (UAW) using
Equation (2). The UAW valuation is contingent upon the various
actors involved. The actors are categorized into three distinct
types (simple, average, and complex) based on the nature and
severity of their challenges.

∗ ∗ ∗
*UAW* = *A* 1 1 + *A* 2 2 + *A* 3 3 (2)

*A* 1 denotes basic actors with a clearly defined application programming interface (API), *A* 2 refers to intermediate actors
communicating through a specific protocol, and *A* 3 represents
advanced actors that communicate using a graphical user interface (GUI). 1, 2, and 3 are the weights corresponding to simple,
average, and complex actors, respectively.

The second component of UCP computation is the determination of unadjusted use case weights (UUCW), which can be derived using Equation (3). The UUCW relies on the utilization of
use cases. Similar to actors, use cases can be categorized into
three classifications, namely, simple, average, and complex,
based on the quantity of transactions involved.

∗ ∗ ∗
*UUCW* = *U* 1 5 + *U* 2 10 + *U* 3 15 (3)

*U* 1 denotes simple use cases with three or fewer transactions,
*U* 2 represents average use cases, encompassing use cases with
transaction counts ranging from 4 to 7, and *U* 3 signifies complex
use cases involving use cases with seven or more transactions. 5,
10, and 15 are the weights corresponding to simple, average, and
complex use cases, respectively.

Then, unadjusted use case points (UUCP) are calculated, as
shown in Equation (4).

*UUCP* = *UAW* + *UUCW* (4)


*Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025 3 of 16

The technical complexity factor (TCF) and environmental complexity factor (ECF) are the third and fourth components of the
UCP calculation. The UUCP value can be adjusted using TCF
and ECF. Thirteen technical complexity characteristics have an
impact on the effectiveness of software projects. The assigned
values for these characteristics span from 0, signifying no influence, to 5, signifying a significant influence. The TCF can be
calculated using Equation (5).


13

*i* = 1


*TCF* = 0.6 + 0.01 [∗] *T* ∗ *W* *t* (5)

the productivity should be computed with the help of data.

**2.1.2** **S&W Modification**

In another study by Schneider and Winters [10], they calibrated
the value of productivity with the help of 8 environmental factors. They divided the productivity values into three classes
(very low = 36, low = 28, and fair = 36) based on environmental
factors. First, they counted the number of factors from *E* 1 to *E* 6
having an influence value lesser than 3. Then, they counted
the number of factors from *E* 7 to *E* 8, having an influence value
greater than 3. Finally, they calculated the total sum by adding
both values. They suggested three levels of productivity based
on the value of the total sum, as shown in Equation (9).


*T* *i* ∗ *W* *t*

weight associated with that factor. Karner [6] identified thirteen
complexity factors, which are distributed system ( *T* 1 ), response
adjectives ( *T* 2 ), end- ­user efficiency ( *T* 3 ), complex processing ( *T* 4 ),
reusable code ( *T* 5 ), easy to install ( *T* 6 ), easy to use ( *T* 7 ), portable
( *T* 8 ), easy to change ( *T* 9 ), concurrent ( *T* 10 ), security feature ( *T* 11 ),
access for third parties ( *T* 12 ), and special training required ( *T* 13 ).
The weights ( *W* *i* *[t]* [) associated corresponding to these thirteen fac-]
tors are 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, and 1, respectively.
Similarly, it is worth noting that eight environmental complexity
elements have the potential to exert an influence on the performance of software projects. The values associated with these
factors are also within the numerical range of 0–5. The ECF
value can be calculated using Equation (6).

**2.1.3** **Nassif's Modification**

Nassif et al. [9] also conducted a study to analyze the effect
of productivity on effort estimation. They assumed that effort
and UCP are related nonlinearly, and their relationship follows an exponential curve. They proposed a nonlinear equation for effort estimation from UCP and productivity, shown
in Equation (10).


*E* *i* ∗ *W* *e*


*i*


∗


*E* *i* represents the environmental factor type, and *W* *i* *[e]* [ denotes the ]
weight associated with that factor. Karner [6] identified eight environmental factors, which are familiar with RUP ( *E* 1 ), application experience ( *E* 2 ), object- ­oriented experience ( *E* 3 ), lead analyst
capability ( *E* 4 ), motivation ( *E* 5 ), special requirements ( *E* 6 ), part- ­
time workers ( *E* 7 ), and different programming language ( *E* 8 ). The
weights ( *W* *i* *[e]* [) associated corresponding to these eight factors are ]

1.5, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 1, 2, 1, and 2, respectively.

The UCP value can be determined by utilizing the equation presented in Equation (7).

*UCP* = *UUCP* [∗] *TCF* [∗] *ECF* (7)

As mentioned in Equation (1), the software effort multiplies
software size and productivity value. Software size (in UCP)
can be obtained from Equation (7). For productivity calculation, Karner [6] conducted a study on three completed industrial software projects. Based on the study's findings, Karner
suggested using a fixed productivity value of 20 person- ­
hours/UCP for organizations with no past data, as shown in
Equation (8).

*Effort* = *UCP* [∗] 20 (8)

Several organizations have used the productivity value suggested by Karner [6] for measuring the effort without knowing
its validity. Utilizing a fixed productivity value is not the right
solution, as each software project's nature and development environment differ. So, using a fixed productivity value for projects


The value of productivity is calculated based on prod_sum
value (prod_sum = [∑] *i* [8] =1 *[E]* *[i]* ∗ *W* *ei* [). They provided this prod_sum ]

value as input to a fuzzy model, which converts it into a productivity value utilizing some predefined rules. They suggested four productivity classes based on the findings of this
study. The prod_sum value of less than 0 indicates a productivity value of 0.4. The prod_sum value in the range of 1 to 10
indicates a productivity value of 0.7. If the prod_sum value is
in the range of 11–20, the value of productivity is 1; else, the
value of productivity is 1.3.

**2.2   |   Related Work and Motivation**

The two important factors for evaluating software effort are size
and productivity [8]. However, most of the studies in the literature are focused on building a model that shows a relationship
between effort and size measures only. The studies related to
productivity estimation are limited. This work focuses on effort
estimation with the help of a productivity factor when the size is
already known. So, studies concerned with the size estimation
model are discarded.

Jorgensen et al. [12] have proposed a method for productivity
prediction by integrating the analogy- ­based estimation method
with the regression toward the mean (RTM) method. Their
approach worked well for the datasets, which are divided into


8.16
*Effort* = *UCP* [1.17] (10)
*productivity*


*UCP* [1.17]


4 of 16 *Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025

subsets depending upon some categorical variable. In Rodriguez
et al. [13], the size and productivity attributes analysis has
been conducted on the International Software Benchmarking
Standards Group (ISBSG) dataset to inspect their usefulness in
SEE. They created subsets of an original dataset based on the
type of development and the programming language used. They
found that enhanced projects are more productive compared to
new projects. Also, the projects with a team size greater than 9
are less productive.

Sentas et al. [14] have developed an ordinal regression (OR)
method for productivity prediction based on independent variables. They have validated the proposed model's performance by
applying it to three datasets (Maxwell, COCOMO, and ISBSG release seven). They found that the proposed model results on the
above- ­reported datasets are comparable with the existing work.
Petersen [15] has organized a systematic literature review utilizing 38 studies for software productivity prediction. They have
shown risks related to the ratio- ­based measurement approaches.
He also found simulation and statistical process control methods to be the most promising software productivity prediction
approaches. He suggested using environmental factors for productivity calculation without historical data.

The studies mentioned above are mostly based on procedurally
developed software, not modern- ­day OO software. The effort estimation techniques for OO software differ from those for procedurally developed software. So, a thorough investigation of OO
software- ­based effort estimation studies is needed.

The size of OO software is generally calculated in terms of UCP.
In 1993, Karner [6] developed a UCP calculation approach with
the help of use case diagram components such as actors and use
cases. The major problem with the Karner's approach was that
it used a fixed productivity value of 20 person- ­hours/UCP for
every project, which is not the right solution as each software
project's nature and development environment are different.
Afterward, researchers modified the Karner's UCP calculation
approach by dividing productivity values into different classes

[9, 10]. Schneider and Winters [10] divided the productivity
values into three classes based on environmental factors. The

major problem with the S&W approach was that the classification technique relied on counting the factors, disregarding the
impact of their values. Nassif et al. [9] also proposed a nonlinear
equation for effort estimation from UCP and productivity. They
derived four productivity levels by giving prod sum value as
input to the fuzzy logic models. However, the results would have
been better if they had used clustering approaches depending on
the gathered data.

Azzeh and Nassif [11] have developed a two- ­stage hybrid model
for effort estimation utilizing productivity and show the utilization of classification and clustering- ­based approaches for deriving different productivity labels. The approach involves using
the K- ­medoid method to divide projects into different clusters
and assign a label to every cluster. Then, the support vector
classifier is used for learning productivity labels, considering
environmental factors as input. Finally, at the testing stage, the
productivity label will be calculated for each testing instance.
The productivity label is assigned a value, which is the medoid
of the cluster associated with that productivity label. Finally,


the size and the calculated productivity values are input to the
radial basis function network to predict the effort value. The
productivity values largely depend upon the technique used to
cluster and classify projects. The same project may lie in other
classes, depending upon the method. So, there is a need for an
approach that learns the value of productivity directly from
environmental factors instead of classifying it into different
classes.

In this study, we proposed a PredictPP model for project productivity prediction with the help of environmental factors. The
motivation behind this approach is that the prediction of project
productivity dynamically varies based on the values of environmental factors, which will ultimately give a better estimation of
software efforts than choosing the productivity value from some
set of values, as done in traditional methods. The proposed approach and other models have also been compared to obtain the
best performing model, which is further compared with the existing UCP prediction models in the literature.

**3   |   Proposed Approach**

As mentioned earlier, the UCP approach for SEE consists of size
estimation (in terms of UCP) and effort estimation with the help
of calculated UCP. The size estimation is not the focus of this
paper. The software size can be easily calculated with a well- ­
defined procedure by Karner [6]; we are only interested in predicting productivity values. Further, the predicted productivity
values can be used to estimate the value of effort.

**3.1   |   Underlying Fundamental**

Few studies have reported the use of project productivity for
SEE using a restricted number of productivity values [6, 9, 10],
as shown in Figure 1. The major problem with these methods
is that they used only static values for project productivity.
However, we used learning techniques to predict productivity in
the proposed method, considering past projects as input.

Schneider and Winters [10] demonstrated that environmental
factors such as team experience, team members' capabilities,
and knowledge about projects can contribute more efficiently to
productivity prediction. Also, evaluating these factors is simple
and requires minimal expertise. So, in this study, we use environmental adjustment factors for productivity prediction, as
shown in Figure 2.

**FIGURE 1** |    Illustration of the existing approaches for UCP

estimation.


*Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025 5 of 16

Firstly, the eight environmental factors are input to the learning model for productivity prediction. Then, the effort will
be calculated with the help of size and predicted productivity
value. Figure 3 shows the methodology for creating the proposed PredictPP model, as discussed in detail in upcoming

sections.

**3.2   |   Level 1: Base Learner Selection**

The first stage, Level 1, encompasses selecting the base learners.
The selection of these base learners is crucial for creating ensemble models that may be effectively used. The efficacy of this
selection method relies on the degree to which the model aligns
with the dataset and its ability to generate accurate predictions.
Therefore, the individual models are implemented, evaluated,
and selected based on different performance metrics. An experiment was conducted wherein eight distinct learning models
were applied to a dataset of 65 Western University software projects [9] to determine appropriate base learners for ensemble formation. This experiment aims to select base learners from a pool
of regularly employed learning models for the PredictPP model,
which is proposed for productivity prediction. We have chosen
SLR, LR, RR, ER, KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP learning models for
this experimental analysis.

This analysis selects five individual learners (RR, KNN, DT,
SVR, and MLP) as the base learners. Section 4 provides a comprehensive experiment analysis and a concise overview of the
chosen base learners.

**FIGURE 2** |    Illustration of the proposed approach for UCP estimation.

**FIGURE 3** |    Framework for the proposed PredictPP model.


**3.3   |   Level 2: Creating Homogeneous Ensemble**
**Learners**

Level 2 entails constructing homogeneous ensemble prediction
models from the base learners (RR, KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP)
through bagging [16] and boosting [16] techniques. Ten different
homogeneous ensemble prediction models are constructed at
this stage, consisting of the bagging RR, bagging KNN, bagging
DT, bagging SVR, bagging MLP, boosting RR, boosting KNN,
boosting DT, boosting SVR, and boosting MLP ensembles. The
performance of these ensemble models is evaluated separately
on the given dataset to assess their effectiveness. The performance of these ensemble models is assessed using the leave- ­
one- ­out cross- ­validation (LOOCV) strategy.

This analysis selects the top three ensemble learners (bagging
KNN, boosting DT, and boosting SVR) to create a rank- ­based
weighted ensemble learner. The methodology for assigning
weights is discussed in the next section. Section 4 provides a
comprehensive examination of the experimental analysis and a
concise portrayal of the chosen ensemble learners.

**3.4   |   Level 3: Meta- ­Learner for Assigning Weights**
**to Ensemble Learners**

At this stage, a meta- ­learner allocates weights to the ensemble
learners derived from Level 2. The proposed method utilizes a
ranking average mechanism as a meta- ­learner to allocate the
weights to the selected ensemble learners. First, sort the selected


6 of 16 *Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025

ensemble learners based on their error values in descending
order, that is, the model with the highest error value will be assigned rank one, and so on. Then, assign weights to the selected
three ensemble learners using Equation (11):

under consideration from a list of given values. We have used
the GridSearchCV function from the Scikit- ­learn library to
implement grid search.

**4.1   |   Dataset Used**

We performed an in- ­depth review of datasets pertaining to the
UCP- ­based estimate and discovered six related datasets: DS1 to
DS6. DS1 consists of 240 industry and academic software projects gathered from four primary sources [17]. DS2 comprises
84 projects sourced from three distinct sources [18], whereas
DS3 encompasses 28 projects [19]. DS4 comprises 71 projects
provided by three data donors [19]. DS5 encompasses 65 software academic projects from Western University [9], whereas
DS6 consists of 45 projects from the CompuTop company [9].

As mentioned earlier, the UCP estimation approach consists of
two key stages: size estimation (in terms of UCP) and effort estimation with the help of calculated UCP. A significant amount
of research has already been done for size estimation utilizing
DS1, DS2, DS3, and DS4 datasets. However, size estimation
is not the focus of this paper. Our research especially focuses
on the second phase—predicting effort, when the project size
(UCP) is already established. The effort estimation using UCP is
widely explored, which requires various factors along with UCP.
One such factor is project productivity, which is to be used with
UCP for effort estimation. As discussed earlier, this paper aims
to ultimately help in improved effort estimation by predicting
project productivity based on various environmental factors.
The datasets mentioned above (DS1, DS2, DS3, and DS4) cannot
be considered for productivity prediction as they do not contain
any information about environmental factors.

Among the listed datasets, only DS5 (or Western University
dataset) is publicly accessible for research purposes. Because
the Western University dataset is public and pertinent to the
estimation of UCP- ­based effort, this dataset is the main empirical source for our investigation. So, we used only the Western
University dataset for the experiment. The Western University
dataset contains projects that were created and executed utilizing UML and OO languages. The dataset comprises ten features:
size, environmental factors (E1 to E8), and effort. Productivity
values for projects in the dataset are calculated by dividing the
effort by the software size, as shown in Equation (1).

Although the Western University dataset predominantly comprises academic software projects, which may differ in terms
of complexity and development environment from industrial
projects, the PredictPP model is fundamentally designed to
capture and learn from environmental factors—such as team
experience, project complexity, and technical familiarity—that
are also highly relevant within industrial contexts. Moreover,
the methodology itself is model- ­agnostic and can be readily applied to industrial datasets when such data become available.
The statistical properties of the dataset are shown in Table 1.

The dataset's statistical properties show that the dataset's productivity values are approximately symmetric, with a skewness
value of 0.176. The productivity values are positively skewed,
with the kurtosis value of −0.3157.

*Productivity* [(] *y* *j* ) = ∑ *EL* *i* ( *y* *j* ) ∗ *W* ( *EL* *i* ) (12)


*EL* *i*


( *y* *j*


) ∗ *W* ( *EL* *i*


Here, *EL* *i* ( *y* *j* ) represents the predicted productivity value for the
project *y* *j* using ensemble learners *EL* *i* .

Detailed steps for implementing the PredictPP approach are presented in Algorithm 1.

In Algorithm 1, we divided the dataset of n software projects
into n parts and executed the model for n rounds. For every
round, *n* − 2 parts are used as a train set, one as a validation
set, and one as a test set. The final result will be the average
result of n rounds. Eight individual learning models (SLR, LR,
RR, ER, KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP) have been applied over the
training dataset, and the trained models are validated using
a validation dataset to choose the top five base learners (RR,
KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP). The top five base learners are then
used to create ten homogeneous ensemble learners (bagging
RR, bagging KNN, bagging DT, bagging SVR, bagging MLP,
boosting RR, boosting KNN, boosting DT, boosting SVR, and
boosting MLP). The ten ensemble learners are also analyzed to
obtain the top three homogeneous ensemble learners (bagging
KNN, boosting DT, and boosting SVR) that create a proposed
PredictPP model for effort estimation. The methodology for assigning weights to the top three ensemble learners is discussed
in Section 3.4. After weight assignment, the productivity predictions for the testing data are made using Equation (12).

learning approaches have been implemented utilizing the
Scikit- ­learn module in the Python programming language.
We have applied a LOOCV technique for building the learning
models. The hyperparameters of various base learners are decided based on the grid search approach. The grid search approach provides the best set of parameter values for the model

**4.2   |   Performance Evaluation Measures**

Performance measures are employed to assess various learning models. However, selecting them is not straightforward
due to the potential for overestimation or underestimation,
as noted in previous research [20]. Most studies have utilized


mean magnitude relative error (MMRE) and prediction accuracy (Pred) measures to assess the proposed model's performance. However, these measures are known as biased
measures, especially MMRE, due to their sensitive nature
toward outliers [20]. So, we utilize the other measures, such
as mean absolute error (MAE), mean balanced relative error

in brief in Table 2. These measures are selected as they are
frequently used in the literature to evaluate productivity prediction models [9, 21–24].

In addition to these measures, we conducted a systematic error
directionality assessment to examine whether the PredictPP
model exhibits any consistent bias—that is, a tendency to overestimate or underestimate productivity. For this purpose, we
computed the mean error (ME), which considers the signed
difference between predicted and actual values. Unlike MAE,
which measures only the magnitude of the error, ME helps identify the direction of prediction errors.

**4.3   |   Choosing the Base Learners**

The learning approaches employed in this study are advantageous in their ability to effectively extract inherent patterns from
the input data and establish correlations between these input
features and the corresponding output. Moreover, the acquired
data can be employed to predict the outcome of new projects.
Various machine learning (ML) algorithms have been employed
in previous studies for UCP estimation and productivity prediction. The SLR [9, 17, 18, 22, 25–27] is the most frequently used
ML model for UCP estimation and productivity prediction due
to its efficacy. Nevertheless, the assumptions of the SLR do not
always hold. In such scenarios, the regularization techniques,
such as LR, RR, and ER, provide more flexibility, robustness,
and performance. So, we have expanded our research by integrating modified versions of the SLR model that use regularization techniques. Some existing studies have utilized the
MLP [9, 22, 24], SVR [22, 24], and DT [22, 24] models for productivity prediction. Apart from these models, the KNN model
is frequently employed for regression problems. Nevertheless,
previous studies on UCP estimates have not examined the KNN

experimental analysis.

To assure optimal performance of individual learners, such as
SLR, LR, RR, ER, KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP, we used a grid
search- ­based hyperparameter tuning technique. The primary
goal is to find the best combination of hyperparameter values
that maximizes prediction accuracy while being computationally efficient. We discovered that certain hyperparameters,
such as the regularization parameter (C) in SVR, the number of
neighbors (k) in KNN, and the hidden layer sizes in MLP, had a
significant impact on model performance, whereas others had
a minor impact and thus were kept at their default values to reduce computational overhead without sacrificing model quality.
This selective tuning strategy enables us to strike a compromise
between exhaustiveness and efficiency in model optimization.

demonstrates superior performance compared to other individual learning models. The KNN model with an MAE value of

DT model with an MAE value of 260.95 is the third best individ
ual model. The top five base learners for the proposed PredictPP
approach are RR, KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP.

learners creating the ensemble learner may or may not be the
same type. The two main reasons for using ensemble methods
are performance and robustness. The ensemble learner can perform better than the individual learners, reducing the variance of
predictions. So, we have created different homogeneous ensemble

**4.5   |   Experimental Results**

The top three ensemble learners (bagging KNN, boosting DT,
and boosting SVR) are used to generate predictions for the
proposed PredictPP model. The proposed ranking method
(Section 3.4) is used to assign weights to the ensemble learners.
The boosting SVR model is assigned the highest weight (0.5) as it
is the best performing model among the three models. Similarly,
the boosting DT model is assigned the lowest weight (0.16).
The bagging KNN model weighs 0.34. We have also analyzed
the classical models. Table 7 shows the comparative results of
the top five base learners, the top three homogeneous ensemble
learners, and the proposed PredictPP model.

Table 7 shows that the proposed PredictPP model has outperformed all models based on different error measures. The MAE

value obtained from the proposed model is 228.2332. In addition, the ME value for the proposed model was found to be very
close to zero, indicating a balanced error distribution.


**5   |   Comparative Analysis**

**5.1   |   Comparison Using Statistical Analysis**

In the earlier section, error estimates for various models were
shown. The findings indicate that the PredictPP model, as suggested, has satisfactory performance. However, it is imperative to validate the accuracy and reliability of these models. In
this segment, we have performed statistical analysis using the
Wilcoxon test [29] to investigate these models' characteristics.
The nature of the two distributions, following similar or dissimilar patterns, can be inspected with the Wilcoxon test. The subsequent hypothesis is employed to examine the characteristics
of two distributions:

  - *H* 0 : Lack of substantial differentiation between models A
and B.

  - *H* 1 : Models A and B are significantly different.

The hypothesis mentioned above is predicated upon the utilization of the *p* value. A *p* value beyond 0.05 supports the acceptance of hypothesis *H* 0, whereas a *p* value below 0.05 supports
the acceptance of hypothesis *H* 1 . Table 8 displays the outcomes
of the Wilcoxon test.

Table 8 shows that the Wilcoxon signed rank test indicates the
overall advantage of PredictPP; nevertheless, the *p* values for
SVR (0.4864) and boosting SVR (0.5283) are not statistically
significant at the level of 0.05. This indicates that, although
PredictPP demonstrates superior average performance, variations with these two baselines are insufficient to be deemed

statistically significant. We present these findings for the
sake of thoroughness and to offer an impartial analysis of the
results.

**6.1   |   Answers to RQs**

This section responds to the research questions (RQs) previously
mentioned.

**RQ1** . *How does the proposed PredictPP model perform*
*compared to the base models to predict the value of project*
*productivity* ?

To answer RQ1, we have compared the performance of the
proposed PredictPP model with the top five base models (RR,
KNN, DT, SVR, and MLP) in this work. The evaluation and
comparison of the proposed approach is done over the original
dataset of 65 projects with the help of five different performance
measures. The PredictPP model performed better than the top
five base learning models, as shown in Table 7. The MAE value
obtained from the PredictPP model is 228.23, whereas the MAE
value for the best performing base learning model (SVR) is
252.73. The other base models have MAE values between 259.94

and 267.76.

**RQ2** . *Does the proposed PredictPP model generate better pre-*
*dictions than other homogeneous ensemble learning models* ?

To answer RQ2, we have compared the performance of the proposed PredictPP model with the top three ensemble learning
models (bagging KNN, boosting DT, and boosting SVR) over
the original dataset of 65 projects with the help of five different performance measures. The results show an improvement
in MAE values after applying the proposed PredictPP model, as
shown in Table 7. The MAE value obtained from the PredictPP

model is 228.23, whereas the MAE value for the best performing base learning model (boosting SVR) is 236.70. The bagging
KNN and boosting ensembles have MAE values of 248.76 and
250.02, respectively.

**6.2   |   Computational Considerations and Efficiency**

Ensemble learning techniques enhance predictive performance
but typically incur additional computational complexity, particularly with dynamic weighting, repeated resampling, or
complicated structures like boosting or stacking. This study intentionally developed the PredictPP rank- ­based ensemble model
to ensure both performance and computing efficiency, considering practical limitations and the deployment requirements of
industrial settings.

In contrast with traditional ensemble methods like dynamic
bagging or boosting, which involve iterative training or sequential updates of several models, PredictPP allocates fixed weights
to base learners according to their ranked performance on validation data. This ranking is calculated once during training,
hence eliminating the need for repeated evaluation or weight
modification during prediction. The computational overhead
during inference is negligible, rendering the model appropriate
for real- ­time applications and incorporation into ongoing development workflows.

To enhance model performance while minimizing computing demands, we employed a grid search method to adjust just
the most significant hyperparameters of the base learners.
Parameters with minimal impact on performance were maintained at their default settings. This method achieved an optimal
balance between model performance and training cost.

The PredictPP framework provides a streamlined and scalable
approach for estimating software productivity. Its minimal inference time and single- ­pass prediction capacity render it suitable
for industrial applications, particularly those necessitating rapid


decision- ­making or functioning under resource limitations.
These attributes establish PredictPP as a feasible substitute for

more intricate ensemble models, providing better performance
while maintaining operational efficiency.

Although the proposed predictPP model is inherently industry- ­
agnostic, we understand that its implementation across extensive industrial teams may pose difficulties. The efficacy of the
proposed model is contingent upon the accessibility of high- ­
quality historical data, which might differ substantially among
large enterprises with decentralized teams. Furthermore, incorporating estimates into current project management workflows may necessitate further adjustments to accommodate
differences in team productivity, communication overhead,
and organizational procedures. These elements emphasize the
need to customize the model for industrial contexts and verify
its efficacy on extensive datasets derived from actual software
projects.

**6.3   |   Practical Implications for Practitioners**

The PredictPP model, although methodologically sound, provides considerable practical benefits for software project managers and industry professionals engaged in the beginning stages
of estimation. The model is explicitly developed for seamless
integration with the prevalent UCP sizing methodology and
may be readily included in current estimation processes. To
implement PredictPP in practice, the subsequent steps can be
undertaken:

1. Data collection: During the requirements analysis phase,
practitioners collect the eight basic environmental variables outlined in the UCP approach. These encompass variables such as team expertise, application complexity, tool
knowledge, and development limitations.

2. Input to PredictPP: Environmental variables serve as
input for the trained ensemble model of PredictPP. The
model analyzes this information and provides a predicted
productivity.

3. Effort estimation: The predicted productivity is multiplied
by the overall size (UCP) of the software project to calculate the final estimated effort.

4. Deployment options: The PredictPP model is efficient and
adaptable, facilitating effortless integration across diverse
environments, including Python or R scripts for technical
teams, web- ­based APIs linked with project management
platforms like Jira, Redmine, or MS Project, and customized dashboards designed for estimation teams.

1. Efficiency: In contrast to complicated ensembles that necessitate dynamic weighting for each instance, PredictPP
employs a rank- ­based static weighting system, therefore
considerably diminishing processing demands during
prediction.

2. Reproducibility and simplicity: The model's architecture,
built on established base learners and coupled with a clear
rank- ­weighted aggregation, facilitates straightforward implementation, maintenance, and explanation.


*Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025 13 of 16

3. Scalability and generalization potential: This work used
a dataset of academic software projects; nonetheless, the
PredictPP approach is fundamentally modular and generalizable. It is applicable to any dataset where project sizing metrics are accessible (e.g., UCP and function points),
environmental or contextual variables of projects can be
measured, and effort or productivity measurements can be
captured.

Additionally, in this study, UCP was selected as the sizing metric because it corresponds with our research objectives and the dataset's structure. The dataset offers
clearly delineated UCP- ­based effort estimates alongside relevant environmental and technical complexity
variables, which are essential inputs for the PredictPP
algorithm.

UCP provides a systematic and measurable methodology based on OO analysis, rendering it especially appropriate for early- ­stage effort estimation [9]. Compared to
alternatives, function points necessitate comprehensive
design- ­level knowledge, whereas story points tend to be
dependent upon team dynamics and subjective interpretation. Conversely, UCP incorporates standard adjustment
variables and facilitates more consistent, objective modeling throughout the early stages of development. Thus,
UCP not only improves the methodological rigor of our
approach but also enables more dependable productivity
prediction based on early- ­stage requirements.

4. Interpretability of the PredictPP model: PredictPP is designed to establish a balance between predictive power
and model interpretability. One significant method we
used was a rank- ­based weighting mechanism that assigned
static, data- ­driven significance values to each base learner.
This transparent ranking system enables practitioners to
readily understand each model's relative contribution to
the overall ensemble output. Unlike black- ­box ensembles,
which rely on dynamically modified weights or meta- ­
learners, this technique provides intuitive insights into
model behavior.

Furthermore, the individual base learners utilized in PredictPP
are inherently interpretable models. Their inclusion guarantees that the ensemble's decision- ­making process is based
on models whose internal logic can be comprehensibly interpreted by domain specialists.

PredictPP retains explainability by combining a simple
ranking- ­based aggregate with interpretable constituent
models, which is frequently lost in more sophisticated ensemble frameworks. This makes it a practical and clear solution for real- ­world applications where model knowledge is
equally important as predicted accuracy.

The PredictPP approach has numerous practical benefits for industry practitioners:

Estimating productivity is crucial for helping managers measure
project metrics in real- ­world scenarios. It facilitates distributing
resources, planning projects, creating budgets, assessing performance, and managing risks. Accurate productivity estimates empower managers to optimize resource allocation by identifying


the necessary number of developers for a project, which guarantees the most efficient use of resources. Furthermore, estimating productivity enables more accurate scheduling of project
timeframes and milestones, facilitating the establishment of
realistic deadlines and expectations based on team productivity
estimations, which minimizes the probability of missing deadlines or project setbacks. Productivity estimation also aids in
budgeting and cost estimation for the project. Managers can determine the labor expenses related to the project by considering
the anticipated productivity of team members, resulting in more
precise project budgets. Further, productivity estimation serves
as a standard for assessing the effectiveness of the development
team. Managers might assess the disparity between actual and
predicted productivity to pinpoint areas that require enhancement or to recognize team members who have achieved exceptional performance. Managers can detect potential dangers early
in the project life cycle by comprehending productivity levels.
If the estimated productivity is below expectations, managers
might adopt proactive actions, such as offering supplementary
training or resources, to mitigate risks and guarantee the project's success.

**7   |   Threats to Validity**

This segment delineated several potential hazards that can
compromise the integrity and reliability of findings. The risks
mentioned above can be categorized into three distinct classifications, namely, internal, external, and construct.

**7.1   |   Internal Validity**

It ensures the degree of conclusions of the study concerning the
arrangement. ML models have been used in this study for productivity prediction and effort estimation. No single ML model
can be used for all the datasets. So, in this study, we have utilized seven different ML models to predict project productivity.
We have also utilized LOOCV and grid search to optimize the
parameters of the models used in this study. Apart from that, we
used the Wilcoxon test to validate the results of these models.

So, we can say that the results provided by these ML models are
validated up to an extent.

**7.2   |   External Validity**

It ensures whether the results provided by the study are generalizable or not. The UCP estimation model mainly relies on the
use case diagrams. The components of a use case diagram, such
as actors and use cases, are transformed into their corresponding size measures to calculate the UCP value using a clearly
defined approach. But the use case diagrams depend upon the
knowledge of the designers. If these diagrams are not designed
properly, they will affect the model's performance. Also, most
of the dataset's projects are academic [9]. The students develop
these projects as their part- ­time work. As industrial projects are
less, the educational projects are utilized to estimate the actual
software's effort. The projects developed by untrained and unskilled students might lead to errors when estimating real industrial software effort because the students focus on the coding


14 of 16 *Journal of Software: Evolution and Process,* 2025

phase of the project while ignoring the other phases of the software development life cycle. Due to these reasons, we are not
sure about the generalizability of the results.

**7.3   |   Construct Validity**

It guarantees that we are estimating what we planned to estimate. In the past, researchers have utilized MMRE and Pred
measures most frequently. However, these measures are known
as biased measures, especially MMRE, due to their sensitive nature toward outliers. In this study, we have utilized some other
robust measures, such as MAE, MBRE, MIBRE, SA, and Δ, to
overcome the asymmetric measures.

**8   |   Conclusion**

A project's productivity is one of the main components for estimating effort using the UCP method. However, static productivity values are utilized in the early UCP methods. We can use
learning techniques to learn productivity from environmental
factors instead of static values. This work presents a novel productivity prediction model called PredictPP, which uses flexible
productivity values for UCP estimation. The proposed model is
built using different individual and ensemble learners. We have
compared the proposed model's performance with the classical
UCP models, base learners, and homogeneous ensemble learners. It was observed that the proposed model exhibited superior performance across several error measures, surpassing all
other models. We also performed a statistical analysis using the
Wilcoxon test to validate the various models used in this study.
Further, we used the existing approaches in the literature, compared the proposed PredictPP approach with them, and found
that the performance improved significantly. The findings derived from our investigation are both motivating and indicative
of potential improvements in effort estimation. We suggest including environmental factors only for the productivity calculation instead of using them for UCP estimation. The results
obtained through this study motivate managers to see how they
can better measure environmental factors, as they directly affect
productivity.

A future study is planned to improve ensemble learning algorithms for predicting project productivity, which involves
exploring different ensemble methodologies, fine- ­tuning hyperparameters, and incorporating novel algorithms to improve
the accuracy of predictions. Additionally, we plan to collect and
analyze larger and more diverse datasets, with a particular emphasis on industrial datasets sourced from real software development projects. This increased data collection will yield a more
comprehensive evaluation of the model's effectiveness across
many scenarios and improve its generalizability. We aim to enhance the robustness and practical applicability of the proposed
model by incorporating data that reflects the complexities and
unique characteristics of industrial environments. Further, it
is also planned to incorporate the productivity prediction technique into current project management tools, making it easier
to streamline effort estimation in real- ­world situations, enabling
project teams to make data- ­based decisions and efficiently allocate resources.
